items.hint1: Recall the ranks used to classify living things, starting with kingdom and ending with species, and find where genus sits in that list.
items.hint2: Chordata is a phylum and Mammalia is a class. Both are far bigger groups than a genus, holding many different kinds of animal.
items.hint3: Man's scientific name has two words. One is the genus and the other is the species. Which of the two words comes first in a scientific name?
items.solution:
Answer: C. homo

Every species is given a two-part scientific name, a system called binomial nomenclature. The first word is the genus and the second word is the species. Man is Homo sapiens, so man's genus is Homo.

How to tell: write out the ranks for man, biggest group first.
Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Mammalia
Order: Primates
Family: Hominidae
Genus: Homo
Species: sapiens

Why not the others:
A. chordata: this is man's phylum, a huge group that also includes fish, frogs and birds.
B. mammalia: this is man's class, the group of all animals that feed their young on milk.
D. sapiens: this is the species name, the second word of the scientific name, not the genus.

Exam tip: in any scientific name, the genus comes first and starts with a capital letter, and the species comes second and starts with a small letter. Mangifera indica, the mango, splits the same way: genus Mangifera, species indica.

items.hint1: Look at the overall body shape and the length of the antennae before anything else.
items.hint2: Mosquitoes have no nymph stage at all, and a grasshopper nymph has hind legs much larger than its front legs.
items.hint3: Of the two insects left, which one has a flat oval body and very long antennae?
items.solution:
Answer: D. cockroach

A nymph is the young stage of an insect that develops by incomplete metamorphosis. It already looks like a small, wingless version of the adult, so its body plan tells you which insect it is.

How to tell: the body in the diagram is flattened and oval, the antennae are very long and thread-like, the legs are slim and spiny for running, and there are two short tail feelers (cerci) at the back end. There are no thick jumping legs. That is the cockroach body plan.

Why not the others:
A. grasshopper: its nymph has large, powerful hind legs for jumping. The legs here are slim running legs.
B. mosquito: it develops by complete metamorphosis, through a larva and a pupa, so it has no nymph stage.
C. termite: its nymphs are pale and soft-bodied, with short, bead-like antennae.

Exam tip: in 'identify the nymph' questions, check the hind legs first. Enlarged hind legs point to a grasshopper. Slim running legs with long antennae and a flat oval body point to a cockroach.

items.hint1: Look at the nymph's body covering. It is a hard exoskeleton, and a hard case cannot stretch. Think about what that means for an animal that needs to get bigger.
items.hint2: Respiration and locomotion both carry on after the insect becomes an adult. The question wants a process tied to growing up.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is a feature of every living thing at every age. The other is how a young insect gets round a hard covering that cannot stretch. Which one is a growth process?
items.solution:
Answer: C. moulting

An insect's body is covered by a hard exoskeleton made of chitin, which cannot stretch. To grow, the nymph must shed its old exoskeleton and form a new, larger one. This shedding is called moulting, or ecdysis. A cockroach nymph moults several times, getting bigger each time, and its full adult wings appear only after the last moult.

How to tell: the question asks for a growth process that happens before the adult stage. The nymph in the diagram is small and has no wings yet, so it still has growing to do, and an insect can only grow by moulting. The other three options carry on into adult life, and none of them makes the insect bigger.

Why not the others:
A. respiration: it goes on in every living cell throughout life and releases energy. It does not make the insect bigger.
B. locomotion: it is movement of the whole body from place to place, which the adult does too. It does not make the insect bigger.
D. sensitivity: it is the ability to respond to changes around it, a feature of all living things at every age.

Exam tip: whenever a question links an insect or any other arthropod to growth, think of the hard exoskeleton. Arthropods can only increase in size by moulting, which is why their growth curve rises in steps instead of a smooth line.

items.hint1: Start with the labels that are easiest to read: the one at the very tip of the leaf and the one where the leaf stalk joins the stem.
items.hint2: The tip of a leaf is its apex. The angle between the leaf stalk and the stem, where a small bud grows, is the axil.
items.hint3: Only two options fit I and IV. Between them, check that each label is given a different part of the leaf. Remember that the flat blade of a leaf has more than one name.
items.solution:
Answer: D. apex, midrib, lamina, axil

A simple dicot leaf like the one drawn has a pointed tip called the apex and a flat green blade called the lamina. A main vein, the midrib, runs down the centre, with side veins branching from it. The leaf is joined to the stem by a stalk called the petiole, and the angle between the petiole and the stem, where a bud grows, is the axil.

How to tell: read the easy labels first. I points to the pointed tip, so it is the apex. IV points to the angle where the leaf stalk meets the stem, with a small bud in it, so it is the axil. Only C and D begin with apex and end with axil. C calls II the lamina and III the blade, but lamina and blade are two names for the same part, so they cannot be two different labels. In D, II is the midrib: its line ends on a vein, and the midrib is the main vein that all the side veins branch from. III ends in the flat green tissue between the veins, which is the lamina.

Why not the others:
A. vein, apex, midrib, stalk: I is at the tip of the leaf, so it cannot be a vein, and IV is the axil, not the stalk.
B. midrib, petiole, margin, stalk: I is the tip, not the midrib, and petiole and stalk are two names for the same part.
C. apex, lamina, blade, axil: lamina and blade are the same part of the leaf, so a diagram cannot label them separately.

Exam tip: in labelling questions, name the easiest labels first and cross out every option that disagrees. Then watch for options that give two names to one part, such as lamina and blade, or petiole and leaf stalk.

items.hint1: Xylem and phloem are the plant's transport tissues. Think about how water reaches every part of a leaf.
items.hint2: In a leaf, xylem and phloem run side by side in vascular bundles. These bundles are what you see as the midrib and the veins.
items.hint3: The apex is only the tip, and the axil is the angle where the leaf stalk meets the stem. Of the two labels left, which one ends on a vein rather than on the green tissue between the veins?
items.solution:
Answer: B. II

Xylem carries water and mineral salts into the leaf, and phloem carries the food made in the leaf out to the rest of the plant. In a leaf the two tissues run together in vascular bundles, which lie inside the midrib and veins you can see on the leaf surface.

How to tell: find the label that ends on a vein. II is that label, and question 4 names it the midrib, the main vein of the leaf. The midrib and the veins contain the vascular bundles, so II is where the xylem and phloem are.

Why not the others:
A. I: this is the apex, the pointed tip of the leaf.
C. III: this is the lamina, the flat green tissue between the veins, where most photosynthesis happens.
D. IV: this is the axil, the angle between the leaf stalk and the stem where a bud grows.

Exam tip: in leaves and stems, xylem and phloem run together in vascular bundles. In a leaf, look for the midrib and the veins.

items.hint1: Think about what fills the large vacuole in a plant cell, and what that does to the cell when the vacuole is full.
items.hint2: A vacuole full of cell sap pushes the cytoplasm hard against the cell wall, and the cell becomes turgid. Protection is mainly the job of the cell wall, and sensitivity is not one of the jobs the syllabus gives to the vacuole.
items.hint3: Two options are left, and they sound alike. One comes from thick, hardened cell walls in tissues such as sclerenchyma. The other comes from cells being swollen with water. Which of the two does the vacuole give?
items.solution:
Answer: C. support

The vacuole holds cell sap, a watery solution of sugars, salts and wastes, and that is its storage job. When it is full, it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall and makes the cell firm, or turgid, and turgid cells packed together hold up the stems and leaves of non-woody plants.

How to tell: a plant that is short of water wilts. Its vacuoles lose water, the cells go soft, and the stem and leaves droop. Water the plant and the vacuoles fill again, the cells become turgid, and the plant stands up. That upright hold is support coming from the vacuole.

Why not the others:
A. protection: in a plant cell this is mainly the job of the cell wall and of outer layers such as the epidermis, not the vacuole.
B. strength: a turgid cell does feel firm, but in the syllabus strength comes from the cellulose cell wall and from strengthening tissues such as collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
D. sensitivity: this is a living thing responding to its surroundings, and it is not one of the functions the syllabus gives to the vacuole.

Exam tip: when an option list offers both strength and support, link the vacuole and turgidity to support, and link the cell wall, collenchyma and sclerenchyma to strength.

items.hint1: Compare the salt concentration of solution III with the concentration inside the cell, then work out which way water will move.
items.hint2: Water moves by osmosis from a weaker salt solution to a stronger one. At 6%, solution III is stronger than the cell's 3%, so the cell loses water, and turgid describes a cell that has gained water.
items.hint3: Two of the remaining words describe a cell that has lost water, and one describes a cell that has burst. A plant cell has a cell wall and an animal cell does not. Which water-loss word belongs to a cell with a wall?
items.solution:
Answer: D. plasmolyzed

Water moves by osmosis across the cell membrane from a weaker solution into a stronger one. A plant cell placed in a solution stronger than its own contents loses water, its vacuole shrinks, and the living contents pull away from the cell wall. This is plasmolysis.

How to tell: the cells are about as strong as a 3% salt solution. Solution III is 6% salt, which is stronger, so it is hypertonic to the cell and water leaves the cell by osmosis. The firm cell wall keeps its shape while the membrane and cytoplasm shrink away from it, which is plasmolysis.

Why not the others:
A. turgid: a plant cell becomes turgid when it takes in water from a weaker solution, such as solution I at 1%.
B. crenated: this is the same loss of water in an animal cell such as a red blood cell, which has no cell wall, so the whole cell shrinks and wrinkles.
C. haemolysed: this is a red blood cell bursting after taking in too much water from a weaker solution, and a plant cell cannot burst because its wall holds it in.

Exam tip: in osmosis questions, compare the solution with the cell first to find which way water moves, then check the cell type. A plant cell becomes turgid or plasmolysed; an animal cell bursts or becomes crenated.

items.hint1: Write out the balanced equation for the aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule.
items.hint2: In the balanced equation, one molecule of glucose reacts with six molecules of oxygen.
items.hint3: Be careful: the equation is written for one glucose molecule, and the question has three. Scale the oxygen up in the same ratio.
items.solution:
Answer: D. 18

In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down completely using oxygen to release energy. The balanced equation fixes the ratio: every glucose molecule needs six oxygen molecules.

How to tell:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy
1 glucose molecule needs 6 oxygen molecules
3 glucose molecules need 3 × 6 = 18 oxygen molecules

Why not the others:
A. 3: this is the number of glucose molecules, not the oxygen they need.
B. 6: this is the oxygen for one glucose molecule only.
C. 12: this is the oxygen for two glucose molecules.

Exam tip: learn the respiration equation with its numbers: 1 glucose, 6 O₂, 6 CO₂, 6 H₂O. Any question about several glucose molecules is then a multiplication, whether it asks about oxygen, carbon (IV) oxide or water.

items.hint1: Think about what the walls of sclerenchyma cells are like, and what walls like that are good for.
items.hint2: Sclerenchyma cells have very thick walls hardened with lignin, and they are dead when mature.
items.hint3: Water conduction is the job of xylem vessels and food transport is the job of phloem. Of the two options left, what would thick, hard, dead cells be good for?
items.solution:
Answer: B. mechanical support

Sclerenchyma cells have very thick cell walls hardened with lignin, and they are dead when mature. Walls like these are strong and stiff, so the tissue gives the plant mechanical support. It occurs as long fibres in stems and as stone cells in hard parts such as the shells of nuts.

How to tell: match the structure to the job. A cell with a thick, hard wall and no living contents cannot store or move food, but it is very good at holding the plant up and keeping it firm.

Why not the others:
A. water conduction: this is done by xylem vessels and tracheids.
C. food storage: this is done by parenchyma, living cells with thin walls, as in a yam tuber.
D. food transport: this is done by phloem sieve tubes, which are living cells.

Exam tip: link each plant tissue to its wall. Thin walls (parenchyma) store food. Walls thickened at the corners (collenchyma) give flexible support. Thick lignified walls (sclerenchyma) give rigid support.

items.hint1: Read the labels on the diagram. Is the thing being taken in a solid particle or a drop of liquid, and is it going into the cell or out of it?
items.hint2: The bacterium ends up inside the cell, so the process takes material in, not out.
items.hint3: Endocytosis is the general name for all taking-in by the cell membrane. It has two specific kinds, one for solids and one for liquids. Which specific kind fits a bacterium?
items.solution:
Answer: A. phagocytosis

Some cells can take in large particles by pushing their cell membrane out around the particle until it is fully enclosed in a vacuole inside the cell. When the particle is solid, such as a bacterium, the process is called phagocytosis, which means cell eating.

How to tell: the first drawing shows a bacterium outside the cell. The second shows the cell membrane folded around it, labelled bacterium engulfed. A solid particle being wrapped up and taken in is phagocytosis.

Why not the others:
B. pinocytosis: this is cell drinking, the taking in of tiny drops of liquid, not a solid bacterium.
C. endocytosis: this is the general name for all taking-in by the membrane, covering both phagocytosis and pinocytosis. The question wants the specific process shown.
D. exocytosis: this moves materials out of the cell, the opposite direction.

Exam tip: when two options are both true but one is general and one is specific, choose the specific one. Solid taken in is phagocytosis, liquid taken in is pinocytosis, and material sent out is exocytosis.

items.hint1: Name the process in the diagram first, then think about which cells in the human body do the same job.
items.hint2: In humans, the cells that engulf and destroy bacteria in this way are a type of white blood cell.
items.hint3: The reproductive system makes sex cells and the nervous system carries messages. Of the two systems left, one moves air and the other moves a liquid tissue around the body. Which one do white blood cells belong to?
items.solution:
Answer: B. circulatory

The process in the diagram is phagocytosis. In humans it is carried out by phagocytes, which are types of white blood cell (neutrophils and monocytes). White blood cells are part of the blood, and blood belongs to the circulatory system, which carries these cells to any part of the body where germs get in.

How to tell: link three steps. Engulfing a bacterium is phagocytosis. Phagocytosis in humans is done by white blood cells. White blood cells are carried in the blood, which is part of the circulatory system.

Why not the others:
A. reproduction: its main work is making sex cells and producing young, not destroying germs.
C. respiratory: its main work is gaseous exchange in the lungs. The germ-eating white cells are counted as part of the blood.
D. nervous: its main work is carrying messages as impulses along neurones.

Exam tip: when a question asks which system a cell belongs to, trace the cell to the tissue it is part of. Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are all part of blood, so they all belong to the circulatory system.

items.hint1: Watch the word not in the question. Three statements describe respiration properly and one does not.
items.hint2: Respiration goes on in every living plant cell all the time, in roots as well as leaves, at night as well as by day.
items.hint3: Energy release and oxygen use are both true of aerobic respiration. Of the two statements left, which one would make respiration impossible in a root buried in dark soil?
items.solution:
Answer: B. light and chlorophyll must be present for it to occur

Respiration is the breakdown of food, mainly glucose, to release energy. Every living plant cell needs energy all the time, so respiration goes on in every living cell, day and night. Light and chlorophyll are needed for photosynthesis, the process that makes food, not for respiration, which uses food up.

How to tell: think of a root cell. It has no chlorophyll and sits in dark soil, yet it is alive and respiring. So a statement that respiration needs light and chlorophyll must be wrong.

Why not the others:
A. it occurs in all plant tissues: acceptable, because every living plant tissue respires to get energy.
C. energy is produced as the end product: acceptable, because releasing energy from food is the whole purpose of respiration.
D. it occurs in the presence of oxygen: acceptable, because aerobic respiration, the main kind in plants, uses oxygen.

Exam tip: in respiration versus photosynthesis questions, picture a root cell in dark soil. It respires but cannot photosynthesise, so any statement that needs light or chlorophyll belongs to photosynthesis.

items.hint1: Hypertonic means more concentrated. Think about the two ways any solution can become more concentrated.
items.hint2: Healthy urine has no blood cells in it, and taking sugar out of a liquid makes it weaker, not stronger.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, check how urea actually gets into the tubule, and think about what the kidney takes back from the filtrate in the largest amount.
items.solution:
Answer: D. much water has been removed from urine

A solution is hypertonic when it holds more dissolved substances per unit of water than another solution. As the filtrate flows along the kidney tubule, most of its water is taken back into the blood. The urea and salts left behind end up in much less water, so urine usually ends up more concentrated than blood.

How to tell: the filtrate starts out at about the same concentration as blood plasma. The kidney then takes back about 99% of its water. Take water away from any solution and whatever is left becomes more concentrated.

Why not the others:
A. urine contains high percentage of all cells: healthy urine has no blood cells, because they are too large to be filtered out in the glomerulus.
B. all traces of sugar have been removed from urine: taking a dissolved substance out makes a liquid less concentrated, not more.
C. urea is actively secreted into the renal tubules: urea gets into the tubule mainly by filtration at the glomerulus, not by active secretion, so this is not why urine is concentrated.

Exam tip: for any question on why a body fluid is more or less concentrated, think about water first. Removing water concentrates a solution and adding water dilutes it. The kidney controls how concentrated urine is mainly by how much water it takes back.

items.hint1: Auxins can be natural, made inside the plant, or synthetic, made in factories. The question wants a natural one.
items.hint2: Florigen is linked to flowering, and aldone is not a plant growth hormone.
items.hint3: Of the two chemical names left, one is sold to farmers as a weedkiller. Which one is made in the tips of shoots and roots?
items.solution:
Answer: A. indole acetic acid

Auxins are plant hormones that control growth, mainly by making cells grow longer. The main auxin made naturally by plants is indole acetic acid (IAA). It is produced in the tips of shoots and roots and moves back to the region just behind the tip, where the cells lengthen.

How to tell: separate natural from synthetic. IAA is made inside the plant. Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D) is made in factories.

Why not the others:
B. dichlorophenoxyacetic acid: this is 2,4-D, a synthetic auxin that farmers use to kill broad-leaved weeds.
C. aldone: this is not a plant growth hormone.
D. florigen: this is the hormone linked with starting flowering, and it is not an auxin.

Exam tip: in plant hormone questions, sort the options into natural and synthetic first. IAA, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene are made by plants. 2,4-D and NAA are made in factories.

items.hint1: The sympathetic nervous system gets the body ready for an emergency, often called fight or flight.
items.hint2: In an emergency the heart speeds up and digestion slows down, so a slower heartbeat and more saliva do not fit.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, think about blood pressure. Which effect would raise it and push more blood to the muscles?
items.solution:
Answer: A. constriction of the arteries

The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action in an emergency, often called fight or flight. It speeds up the heart, raises blood pressure and slows down activities such as digestion that can wait. The parasympathetic system has the opposite effects and calms the body again.

How to tell: ask of each option, would this help in an emergency? Narrowing the small arteries that supply the skin and gut raises blood pressure and sends more blood to the muscles, which helps. The other three options are actions of a calm, resting body.

Why not the others:
B. heartbeat to slow down: this is a parasympathetic effect. Sympathetic action makes the heart beat faster.
C. increase in the secretion of saliva: more saliva helps digestion, a parasympathetic action. Sympathetic action reduces saliva, which is why your mouth goes dry when you are frightened.
D. contraction of the bladder: emptying the bladder is a parasympathetic action. Sympathetic action relaxes the bladder wall.

Exam tip: for autonomic nervous system questions, picture a student being chased by a dog. Anything that helps them run, such as a faster heartbeat, wider pupils, raised blood pressure and more glucose in the blood, is sympathetic. Anything that belongs to resting and digesting is parasympathetic.

items.hint1: Trace the path of sound through the ear, starting outside, and note which parts are in the middle ear.
items.hint2: Sound first makes the eardrum vibrate. The middle ear then passes the vibration along a chain of three tiny bones to the inner ear.
items.hint3: The oval and round windows lie at the far side of the middle ear, next to the inner ear. Of the two bones left, which one is attached to the eardrum?
items.solution:
Answer: D. malleus

Sound waves make the eardrum (tympanic membrane) vibrate. The middle ear carries these vibrations across to the inner ear through three tiny bones, the ossicles, in a fixed order: malleus (hammer), incus (anvil) and stapes (stirrup). The malleus is attached to the inside of the eardrum, so it is the first structure in the middle ear to pick up the vibration.

How to tell: follow the chain in order.
Eardrum → malleus → incus → stapes → oval window → cochlea
The first middle ear structure after the eardrum is the malleus.

Why not the others:
A. oval window: it receives the vibration last, from the stapes, and passes it into the fluid of the inner ear.
B. round window: it bulges outwards to release pressure after the vibration has passed through the cochlear fluid.
C. incus: it is the middle bone of the three, so it gets the vibration second, from the malleus.

Exam tip: learn the hearing pathway as one chain in order, since most questions ask which part comes first, next or last. For the ossicles, remember M, I, S: malleus, incus, stapes, working inwards from the eardrum.

items.hint1: Think about what a fruit needs in order to be carried a long way by water.
items.hint2: A fruit dispersed by water must float for a long time without sinking or rotting.
items.hint3: Every fruit has a pericarp, and extra water inside would make a fruit heavier. Of the two options left, think of the thick husk of a coconut. Which option describes it?
items.solution:
Answer: A. fibrous covering

A fruit dispersed by water has to float and survive in water for a long time. A thick, fibrous covering traps air, which keeps the fruit light enough to float, and a tough, waterproof outer skin stops the seed inside from rotting.

How to tell: picture a coconut washed along a beach. Its husk is thick and made of fibres with air spaces between them. That fibrous husk is what keeps it afloat.

Why not the others:
B. smooth surface: a smooth skin on its own does not make a fruit float.
C. water content: water inside a fruit makes it heavier, which does not help it float.
D. pericarp: every fruit has a pericarp, the fruit wall, so it is not special to water dispersal.

Exam tip: match each dispersal method to its adaptation. Water: fibrous, air-filled, waterproof covering. Wind: wings, hairs or a parachute. Animals: hooks, or juicy, brightly coloured flesh. Explosion: pods that dry out and split open.

items.hint1: The question is about how long a flowering plant takes to complete its life cycle, seed to fruit.
items.hint2: A herb is a plant with a soft, non-woody stem. That describes its structure, not how long it lives.
items.hint3: Perennials live for many years. Of the two options left, one needs two years to produce fruit and the other only one. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: C. annuals

Flowering plants can be grouped by how long they take to complete their life cycle. Annuals grow from seed, flower, produce fruits and seeds, and die, all within one year or one growing season. Maize, rice and cowpea are annuals.

How to tell: the question says the plant grows and fruits within a year. The word annual means yearly, as in an annual event that happens once a year.

Why not the others:
A. biennials: they need two years, making leaves and storing food in the first year and flowering in the second, like carrot and onion.
B. perennials: they live for many years, and most, like mango and orange trees, fruit again and again.
D. herbs: this describes plants with soft, non-woody stems, not how long they live.

Exam tip: link the name to the number of years. Annual, one year. Biennial, two years (bi means two, as in bicycle). Perennial, many years.

items.hint1: Digestion is about making food small enough to pass through the gut wall and be absorbed.
items.hint2: Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break food molecules apart. It never builds anything up.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one contains a mistake about what starch is. Which one describes chemical digestion correctly for proteins and fats as well as starch?
items.solution:
Answer: B. breakdown of complex molecules into simple molecules

Food molecules such as starch, proteins and fats are large, complex and mostly insoluble, so they cannot pass through the gut wall into the blood or lymph. Chemical digestion is the breakdown of these large molecules by enzymes into small, simple, soluble molecules that can be absorbed. Water, vitamins and mineral salts are small enough already, so they are absorbed without being digested.

How to tell: look at the three main examples.
Starch → maltose → glucose
Proteins → amino acids
Fats and oils → fatty acids and glycerol
In every case a complex molecule becomes simple ones.

Why not the others:
A. breakdown of starch into carbohydrates: starch is itself a carbohydrate, and this leaves out proteins and fats.
C. build up of simple insoluble molecules: digestion breaks food down, it does not build anything up.
D. build up of simple soluble molecules into complex insoluble molecules: this describes building up, the opposite of digestion.

Exam tip: digestion turns large molecules into small ones, and usually turns insoluble ones into soluble ones. Any option that says build up, or ends with bigger molecules, describes synthesis, not digestion.

items.hint1: Think about what normally stops the bleeding when you get a cut.
items.hint2: Blood clotting needs proteins such as prothrombin, which the liver can only make with the help of one particular vitamin.
items.hint3: Vitamin A is linked to eyesight and the B vitamins to energy release and nerves. Of the two left, which vitamin is needed for blood to clot?
items.solution:
Answer: A. K

When the skin is cut, the blood forms a clot that plugs the wound. The liver can only make prothrombin and some other clotting factors if the body has enough vitamin K. Without it, blood clots slowly or not at all, and even a small injury can bleed for a long time.

How to tell: link the symptom to the vitamin. Excessive bleeding means clotting has failed, and clotting depends on vitamin K.

Why not the others:
B. E: it protects cells from damage and is linked with fertility, not with clotting.
C. B: the B vitamins help release energy from food and keep nerves healthy. Lack of vitamin B₁ causes beriberi.
D. A: it is needed for good eyesight. Lack of it causes night blindness.

Exam tip: learn each vitamin with its deficiency sign. A, night blindness. B₁, beriberi. C, scurvy with bleeding gums. D, rickets. K, blood that clots slowly. Do not confuse the two kinds of bleeding: scurvy weakens the gums, while lack of vitamin K slows clotting.

items.hint1: Name each labelled organ first. The tube coming down at the top of the drawing is the oesophagus, which carries food down from the mouth.
items.hint2: Saliva has no enzyme for protein. The first protein-digesting enzyme, pepsin, is made by an organ that also makes hydrochloric acid.
items.hint3: Neither III nor IV makes acid or pepsin. Between I and II, which one does the oesophagus open straight into?
items.solution:
Answer: A. I

Protein digestion starts in the stomach. The stomach wall makes gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. Pepsin works best in acid conditions and breaks proteins down into shorter chains called peptides. Saliva in the mouth has no enzyme for protein, so the chemical digestion of protein does not begin until the stomach.

How to tell: in the diagram the oesophagus comes down from the top and opens into the bag labelled I, so I is the stomach. II is the long, speckled organ lying below the stomach (the pancreas), III is the large organ on the left (the liver), and IV is the small sac under the liver (the gall bladder).

Why not the others:
B. II: this is the pancreas. Its enzyme trypsin carries on protein digestion in the duodenum, after it has already started in the stomach.
C. III: this is the liver. It makes bile, which has no enzymes. Bile breaks fats into small droplets.
D. IV: this is the gall bladder, which stores bile and makes no enzymes.

Exam tip: for 'where does digestion begin' questions, remember where the syllabus places the first enzyme for each food. Starch: salivary amylase in the mouth. Protein: pepsin in the stomach. Fat: lipase from the pancreas, working in the duodenum.

items.hint1: Name each labelled organ first from its size, shape and position. Then recall which juices act on fat in the small intestine, and where each juice is made.
items.hint2: Fat is handled in two steps: bile breaks it into tiny droplets, then the enzyme lipase splits the fat in those droplets into fatty acids and glycerol. Find the organ in the diagram that makes bile and the organ that makes lipase.
items.hint3: Ask of each labelled part whether it makes a juice used on fat, only stores one, or makes nothing for fat at all. Keep only the parts that make one. For each, ask whether that organ actually makes a substance that works on fat, or only stores one, or makes juices for other foods.
items.solution:
Answer: C. II and III

Fat is digested mainly in the small intestine, in two steps. Bile breaks large fat drops into tiny droplets, and the enzyme lipase then splits the fat in those droplets into fatty acids and glycerol, so the parts that secrete substances for fat digestion are the organ that makes bile and the organ that makes lipase.

How to tell: in the diagram, I is the bag at the top right where the gullet enters, the stomach. II is the long, thin organ lying just below the stomach, the pancreas. III is the large organ filling the upper left, the liver. IV is the small sac attached to the liver, the gall bladder. The pancreas (II) secretes pancreatic juice, which contains lipase, and the liver (III) secretes bile. That gives II and III.

Why not the others:
A. I, II and III: I is the stomach, whose juice in the syllabus carries pepsin and rennin for protein, plus hydrochloric acid, and none of these digests fat.
B. I and III: it adds the stomach, which does not belong, and it leaves out the pancreas, the main source of lipase.
D. I, III and IV: IV is the gall bladder, which stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the duodenum but does not make it, so it is not counted as secreting bile. This option also adds the stomach and leaves out the pancreas.

Exam tip: when a question asks which organ secretes a substance, choose the organ that makes it, not the one that stores it. The liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores it but does not make it.

items.hint1: Recall what villi look like and where in the gut they are found, then ask what that shape is good for.
items.hint2: Villi give the ileum a huge surface area, and each one carries tiny blood vessels and a lacteal that carry digested food away. In the syllabus, water is taken up mainly in the colon, which has no villi.
items.hint3: Two options mention absorbing nutrients. The difference is whether digestion would fail too. Think about where pancreatic juice and bile do their work, and whether they need villi to do it.
items.solution:
Answer: C. absorption of nutrients only

Villi are tiny finger-like projections on the inner wall of the small intestine, especially the ileum, and they are built for absorption. They give a very large surface area, their lining is only one cell thick, and each one carries blood capillaries and a lacteal that take digested food away.

How to tell: without villi the surface area of the ileum drops sharply, so much less digested food can pass into the blood and lymph. Digestion itself would carry on, because pancreatic juice and bile work on food in the space inside the gut, and intestinal juice comes from glands in the gut wall. In the syllabus, villi are for absorption, so the problem is taken to be with absorbing nutrients only.

Why not the others:
A. digestion of food only: the juices that digest food would still work without villi, and this option leaves out absorption, which is the real problem.
B. absorption of water: the syllabus gives this job mainly to the colon, which has no villi, so water uptake is not what villi are known for.
D. digestion of food and absorption of nutrients: this is the trap, but digestion by pancreatic and intestinal juices, helped by bile, goes on without villi, so the syllabus treats only absorption as affected.

Exam tip: link each part of the gut to its main job: villi to absorption, enzymes and bile to digestion, the colon to water. Then read the options for small words such as 'only' and 'and', because they often decide between two answers that look alike.

items.hint1: To name the relationship between two organisms, ask whether one lives on, feeds on or kills the other, or whether they simply share something. Tridax is a common farm weed.
items.hint2: A predator kills and eats its prey, and an epiphyte grows perched on another plant. Neither describes two plants rooted side by side in the soil.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, one needs a host plant to feed from through special roots pushed into its body. The other needs only a shared supply that is too small for both. Which fits a weed growing beside a crop?
items.solution:
Answer: A. competition

Competition happens when two organisms need the same resource and there is not enough for both. The bean and the Tridax grow side by side on the same farmland, and both need light, water, mineral salts and space. Whatever the Tridax takes, the bean cannot use, so both grow less well than they would alone.

How to tell: neither plant lives on, feeds on or kills the other. They are rooted in the same soil and draw on the same limited supplies. That is competition between two different species, and it is why farmers weed their crops.

Why not the others:
B. predation: a predator kills and eats its prey, and neither plant eats the other.
C. parasitism: a parasite feeds from the living body of its host, as dodder does by pushing suckers into its host's stem. Tridax has its own roots in the soil.
D. epiphytism: an epiphyte grows attached to another plant only for support, like an orchid on a tree branch. Tridax grows in the soil.

Exam tip: to name a relationship between two organisms, ask two questions. Does either one live on or inside the other? Does either one feed on the other? If both answers are no and they use the same limited resource, it is competition.

items.hint1: Picture two very different habitats, a pond and a forest, and ask which conditions act in both of them.
items.hint2: Temperature and light both vary in water as well as on land, so both of them affect land and water habitats alike.
items.hint3: Two factors are left. For each one, ask what it actually measures, and whether that still makes sense at the bottom of a pond as well as in a forest.
items.solution:
Answer: B. humidity

Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. It only has meaning where there is air, so it is a factor of land (terrestrial) habitats and not of water (aquatic) habitats, where organisms are already surrounded by water.

How to tell: test each factor in a pond and in a forest. Temperature changes in both. Light changes in both, and in water it fades with depth. Pressure acts in both: air pressure on land, and water pressure that rises the deeper you go. Humidity is the only one that needs air, so it is the exception.

Why not the others:
A. temperature: it affects life on land and in water alike, and a pond warms by day and cools at night just as the land does.
C. light: plants on land and algae in water both depend on it, and its strength changes with shade on land and with depth in water.
D. pressure: it is often taught as a water factor because it rises with depth, but air pressure also acts on land organisms and is listed among the climatic factors of land habitats.

Exam tip: for questions on which factor does not affect all habitats, test each option in both a pond and a forest. A factor that describes the air, such as humidity, belongs to land habitats; one that describes the water, such as salinity or turbidity, belongs to water habitats.

items.hint1: Look closely at the shape of the instrument and the pattern painted on it, then picture what each option in the list looks like.
items.hint2: A wind vane has a pointer that swings round on a pole, and the hygrometer used in school has two thermometers side by side. Does the drawing show either of those?
items.hint3: Of the two options left, recall which one is a U-shaped glass tube holding mercury and alcohol. Is that what the drawing shows?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Secchi disc

A Secchi disc is a flat, round disc painted in alternating black and white quarters, fixed to a rope or a rod marked in centimetres. It is lowered into a pond, lake or river until it just disappears from view. The depth at that point shows how clear the water is and how far light can reach into it.

How to tell: the drawing shows a disc with two black and two white quarters, on a rod with scale marks, being pushed down into water by hand. The arrow shows the direction it is lowered.

Why not the others:
A. wind vane: it shows wind direction and has a pointer that swings on a pole in the open air.
B. Six's thermometer: it records the highest and lowest temperatures, and it is a U-shaped glass tube holding mercury and alcohol.
D. hygrometer: it measures humidity, the amount of water vapour in the air, and the kind used in school has two thermometers, one with a wet bulb.

Exam tip: for ecological instrument questions, first ask where the instrument is used, in air, water or soil, then match its shape. Secchi disc, water clarity. Rain gauge, rainfall. Wind vane, wind direction. Anemometer, wind speed. Hygrometer, humidity. Six's thermometer, highest and lowest temperatures.

items.hint1: First name the instrument from question 29, then think about what it is designed to measure.
items.hint2: This instrument measures how clear or cloudy something is, by seeing how deep the disc can go before it disappears from view.
items.hint3: On land or grass a disc lying on the surface never disappears, so those two are out. Of the two options left, what does the dotted, shaded area around the disc in the drawing show?
items.solution:
Answer: B. in water

The instrument is a Secchi disc, which measures turbidity: how clear or cloudy water is, and so how far light can get into it. It is lowered until it disappears from view. In muddy water, or water full of plankton, the disc vanishes at a shallow depth. In clear water it can be seen much deeper.

How to tell: in the drawing the disc sits inside the dotted, shaded area, which is the water, and the arrow shows it being pushed deeper.

Why not the others:
A. in the atmosphere: factors in the air, such as wind direction, humidity and temperature, are measured with a wind vane, a hygrometer and a thermometer.
C. on land: soil factors such as pH and temperature are measured with a pH meter or a soil thermometer, and a disc cannot be lowered into solid ground.
D. on grass: grass is a land habitat too, and a disc lying on grass never disappears from view, so there is nothing for it to measure.

Exam tip: the way an instrument is used usually tells you its habitat. One lowered into water and read by sight, like the Secchi disc, measures a water factor. One pushed into the ground, like a soil thermometer, measures soil. One mounted in the open, like a wind vane, measures the air.

items.hint1: Picture the S-shaped growth curve of a population, and find the stage where numbers reach the most the habitat can support.
items.hint2: Carrying capacity is the largest number of fish the pond's food, space and oxygen can support. Once it is reached, the population cannot keep climbing, and it has no reason to keep falling while the pond stays the same.
items.hint3: Two options are left: one describes numbers that keep going up and down, the other numbers that hold level. Which matches the top of the S-shaped curve?
items.solution:
Answer: B. remains unchanged

Carrying capacity is the largest population a habitat can support with the food, space and oxygen it has. When a population reaches it, the birth rate equals the death rate, so the population stops growing and is taken as constant at that level. A real pond may show small ups and downs over the weeks, but they stay close to that level, and the growth curve draws it as a flat line.

How to tell: picture the S-shaped (sigmoid) growth curve. It starts slowly (lag phase), climbs steeply (exponential phase), then levels off into a flat top (stationary phase). Carrying capacity is the height of that flat top, and a flat line means the population is not changing.

Why not the others:
A. alternately increases and decreases: this is the tempting one, since a real population wobbles a little around carrying capacity, but those wobbles balance out and the growth curve shows a flat line, so the population is taken as unchanged.
C. increases only: growth has stopped, because the pond has no spare food or space for more fish.
D. decreases only: a steady fall would mean the pond can no longer support that number, so the population would no longer be at its carrying capacity.

Exam tip: tie carrying capacity to the flat top of the S-shaped curve. At that stage births equal deaths, so the population is taken as constant.

items.hint1: Picture a food chain drawn as a pyramid, with producers at the wide base and top carnivores at the narrow tip.
items.hint2: At each step up a food chain, most of the energy is used in respiration and lost as heat. Only about a tenth passes on.
items.hint3: Producers get their energy from sunlight, and each consumer level gets its energy by feeding on the level below, so no level stands on its own. Of the three options left, which one fits a pyramid that gets narrower as it rises?
items.solution:
Answer: B. energy decreases from the base to the apex of the pyramid

A pyramid of energy shows how much energy passes through each feeding (trophic) level of a food chain. Producers at the base trap the most energy from sunlight. At each step up, most of the energy is used in respiration and lost as heat, or stays in parts that are not eaten, so only about 10% passes on to the next level.

How to tell: suppose the producers trap 1,000 units of energy and about 10% passes up each step.
Producers: 1,000 units
Primary consumers: 100 units
Secondary consumers: 10 units
Tertiary consumers: 1 unit
The energy falls at every level, which is why the pyramid narrows to a point.

Why not the others:
A. energy remains constant across trophic levels: energy is lost at every transfer, so it cannot stay the same.
C. energy increases from the base to the apex of the pyramid: no level can pass on more energy than it received.
D. each trophic level is an independent energy source: producers take in energy from sunlight, and each consumer level gets its energy by eating the level below, so the levels depend on one another.

Exam tip: a pyramid of energy is always upright, never upside down, because energy is lost at every level. Pyramids of numbers and biomass can sometimes be upside down, but a pyramid of energy never can.

items.hint1: Eutrophication is a chain of events. Put the events in order of cause and effect, so that each step causes the next one.
items.hint2: The chain always begins when too many nutrients, such as nitrates and phosphates washed in from fertilisers or sewage, get into the water.
items.hint3: The oxygen runs out because bacteria use it up while decaying dead algae. So in the correct order, must the algal growth come before or after the lack of oxygen?
items.solution:
Answer: B. excessive nitrates → massive algal growth → lack of oxygen → death of aquatic

Eutrophication is the over-enrichment of a water body with nutrients. Nitrates and phosphates, often washed in from farm fertilisers or sewage, feed algae, which grow so fast that they cover the water surface. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aquatic organisms die.

How to tell: each step must cause the next one.
Excess nitrates feed the algae
Massive algal growth, then the algae die and decay
Bacteria decaying the algae use up the oxygen
Lack of oxygen kills fish and other aquatic organisms

Why not the others:
A. heavy mineralization → lack of oxygen → massive algal growth: it puts oxygen loss before the algal growth, but the algae are what cause the oxygen loss.
C. excessive phosphates → lack of oxygen → massive algal growth → death of aquatic organisms: it starts correctly but also puts oxygen loss before the algal growth that causes it.
D. massive algal growth → excessive nitrates → lack of oxygen: it puts the algal growth before the nutrients that cause it.

Exam tip: for any sequence question, check that each step causes the next. In eutrophication the order the syllabus expects is nutrients, algal bloom, death and decay of the algae, oxygen loss, death of aquatic life.

items.hint1: Recall the exact definition of a population, and how it differs from a community.
items.hint2: A community is made up of many different species living together in one place. A population is a narrower group than that.
items.hint3: Count how many different kinds of organism each option names. What does that count tell you about population versus community?
items.solution:
Answer: A. tilapia in a lake

A population is all the organisms of one species living in a particular area at a particular time. Its members can breed with one another. When several different species live together in the same place, they form a community.

How to tell: count the kinds of organism in each option. Tilapia in a lake is one kind of fish in one place. Every other option names two different kinds of organism.

Why not the others:
B. fungus and snails on leaf litter: these are two different kinds of organism, so this is part of a community.
C. bees and butterflies on a flower: these are two different kinds of insect, so this is part of a community.
D. flatworms and roundworms in the gut of an animal: these are two different kinds of worm, so this is part of a community.

Exam tip: population means one species. As soon as an option names two or more kinds of organism together, it describes a community.

items.hint1: Population density tells you how crowded a species is in an area. It compares the number of organisms with the size of the area.
items.hint2: Population density = number of organisms ÷ area. The question calls 1,850 a frequency, but use it here as the number of Ageratum plants.
items.hint3: The area is 100 square metres. Divide, and check carefully where the decimal point lands.
items.solution:
Answer: A. 18.50/m²

Population density is the number of individuals of a species per unit area. It lets you compare how crowded a species is in places of different sizes. The question calls 1,850 the frequency, but in ecology frequency means how often a species turns up across the quadrats sampled, usually given as a percentage. For this calculation, take 1,850 as the number of Ageratum plants counted.

How to tell:
Population density = number of individuals ÷ area
= 1,850 plants ÷ 100 m²
= 18.50 plants per m²
The question writes the area as 100 m, but an area is measured in square metres, so read it as 100 m².

Why not the others:
B. 18.05/m²: this puts the digits after the decimal point in the wrong order. 1,850 ÷ 100 is 18.50.
C. 0.50/m²: this would mean only 50 plants on the whole 100 m².
D. 0.05/m²: this would mean only 5 plants on the whole 100 m².

Exam tip: check a density answer by multiplying back. Density × area should give the number of organisms: 18.50 × 100 = 1,850. If it does not, the decimal point is in the wrong place.

items.hint1: Watch the word not. You are looking for the activity that does not act on the pathogen directly.
items.hint2: Disinfectants and ultraviolet rays both kill microorganisms on surfaces, in water and in the air.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one removes the places where germs and their carriers breed, such as stagnant water. What does the other one change instead: the germ, or the person?
items.solution:
Answer: C. eating balanced diets

To control a pathogen means to kill it, stop it breeding or stop it spreading. A balanced diet keeps the body healthy and helps the immune system fight infection, but it does not kill the pathogen, stop it breeding or stop it spreading, so it is not counted as a way of controlling pathogens.

How to tell: ask of each option, does this act on the germ or its carrier, or is it a general health habit? Only the balanced diet is a general health habit.

Why not the others:
A. exposure to ultraviolent radiation: ultraviolet (UV) rays kill many microorganisms, which is why UV lamps are used to disinfect water and surfaces.
B. use of disinfectants: disinfectants kill germs on floors, toilets and other surfaces.
D. destroying the habitats of pathogens: clearing the places where pathogens and their carriers live, such as stagnant water where mosquitoes breed, stops them spreading.

Exam tip: in disease control questions, separate methods that attack the pathogen or its carrier (heat, chemicals, UV rays, clearing breeding sites) from general health habits such as a good diet and rest. Vaccination also counts as a control method, because it protects against one particular disease.

items.hint1: Each vaccine protects against one particular disease or group of diseases. Think about which disease BCG is linked with, and what kind of germ causes it.
items.hint2: BCG contains a weakened bacterium closely related to the germ it guards against, so the disease it prevents must be caused by a bacterium.
items.hint3: Cholera is prevented mainly by clean water and good sanitation. Of the two diseases left, which one mainly attacks the lungs and causes a long-lasting cough?
items.solution:
Answer: C. tuberculosis

BCG stands for Bacille Calmette-Guérin, named after the two French scientists who developed it. It contains a weakened form of a bacterium closely related to the one that causes tuberculosis (TB). The injection trains the immune system to fight the TB bacterium quickly if the child meets it later. In Nigeria it is given at birth.

How to tell: link the vaccine to its disease. BCG is the TB vaccine, and it leaves the small round scar many people have on the upper arm.

Why not the others:
A. malaria: it is caused by a protozoan, Plasmodium, carried by mosquitoes. BCG gives no protection against it.
B. cholera: it is a bacterial disease spread through dirty water and food, and it is prevented mainly by clean water and good sanitation.
D. diphtheria: it is prevented by a different vaccine, the D in the DPT vaccine, not by BCG.

Exam tip: learn vaccines and diseases as pairs. BCG, tuberculosis. OPV, polio. DPT, diphtheria, whooping cough and tetanus. Measles vaccine, measles.

items.hint1: Think about what trees and their roots do for the ground under a forest.
items.hint2: Cutting down a forest destroys the homes and food of many animals, so any option describing a gain for wildlife is wrong.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, picture heavy rain on bare land where a forest used to be, and think about what the trees did with carbon (IV) oxide. Which option is a real effect?
items.solution:
Answer: B. loss of soil particles

Trees protect the soil. Their leaves break the force of falling rain, their roots bind the soil together, and their fallen leaves cover the ground. When a forest is cut down, rain washes the bare soil away and wind blows it off. This loss of soil particles is soil erosion, the main direct effect of deforestation.

How to tell: think about what the trees were doing before they were removed. Once the roots and leaf cover are gone, little is left to hold the topsoil in place.

Why not the others:
A. creation of new habitats: deforestation mainly destroys habitats. The cleared land may suit a few other species, but that is not its main effect.
C. survival of more species: fewer species survive, because many lose their homes and food.
D. reduction of carbon (IV) oxide in the atmosphere: fewer trees take in less carbon (IV) oxide, and burning the cut trees releases more, so the amount in the air goes up.

Exam tip: for questions on the effects of deforestation, list what the forest was doing before it was cut: covering the soil, giving animals homes and food, taking in carbon (IV) oxide, and giving off water vapour that helps bring rain. Each effect is the loss of one of these.

items.hint1: Start with the meaning of conservation, and what kind of thing it is meant to protect.
items.hint2: In Biology, conservation means using natural resources carefully, protecting them and renewing them where possible, so they last. Soil, water, forests and wildlife are all plainly conserved this way, through good farming, reserves and forest laws.
items.hint3: Two options are left. One is not replaced by nature in any human lifetime once it is used up, and the other is what households throw away. Remember that being impossible to replace is not the same as being impossible to conserve.
items.solution:
Answer: D. domestic wastes

In Biology, conservation is the careful use, protection and renewal of natural resources so that they last for people now and in the future. Domestic wastes are not a natural resource: they are what is left over after use, and they are managed by safe disposal, reducing and recycling.

How to tell: ask of each option whether it is a natural resource we want to keep for the future. Minerals, soil, water, forests and wildlife all are, and the syllabus lists each of them for conservation. Household waste is something we want to get rid of safely, not keep.

Why not the others:
A. mineral resources: this draws students because minerals are not replaced by nature in any human lifetime once used up, but non-renewable does not mean they cannot be conserved, and they are made to last by using less and recycling metals.
B. soil and water: soil is conserved by crop rotation, cover crops, terracing and contour ploughing, and water by protecting its sources from pollution and waste.
C. forest and wildlife: these are conserved through forest reserves, game reserves and national parks, and through laws against over-hunting.

Exam tip: 'cannot be conserved' usually points to something that is not a natural resource at all. Do not confuse non-renewable, which means nature does not replace it in any human lifetime, with cannot be conserved.

items.hint1: Watch the word not. Forest conservation means protecting a forest and using it so that it lasts.
items.hint2: Bush fires burn trees and kill animals, so preventing them is good for a forest.
items.hint3: Sort the three options left into activities that add trees and activities that remove trees.
items.solution:
Answer: A. felling of trees

Forest conservation means protecting forests and using them in a way that lets them last. In the syllabus, activities that add trees or protect the trees already there count as conservation. Felling trees, as the option puts it with no control and no replanting, removes the forest and works against conservation. Controlled felling of a few chosen trees, followed by replanting, can be part of conservation, but the option does not say that.

How to tell: sort the options. Planting seedlings and planting tree crops add trees. Preventing bush fires protects trees. Felling removes trees.

Why not the others:
B. planting seedlings: this replaces lost trees, which is called reforestation.
C. preventing bush fires: this saves trees and wildlife from being burned.
D. planting tree crops: the syllabus counts tree crops such as cocoa, rubber and oil palm as conservation, because they keep a cover of trees on the land and protect the soil.

Exam tip: in 'not suitable' conservation questions, look for the one option that removes or destroys the resource. The others usually add to it or protect it.

items.hint1: Discontinuous variation sorts individuals into clear groups with nothing in between. Continuous variation gives a smooth range of values.
items.hint2: Height can take any value within a range, so it is continuous. Any pair that includes height can go.
items.hint3: Both features in the correct pair must be discontinuous. For the two pairs left, test each feature on its own: can it be sorted into a few fixed groups, or does it need a measuring scale?
items.solution:
Answer: D. fingerprint and blood group

Discontinuous variation sorts individuals into a few clear groups with no in-between forms. It is usually controlled by one or a few genes and is hardly affected by the environment. Continuous variation gives a smooth range of values with many in-between forms, such as height and weight.

How to tell: test each feature on its own. Fingerprints fall into set patterns: arch, loop and whorl. ABO blood groups fall into four set groups: A, B, AB and O. Both features are discontinuous, so the pair works.

Why not the others:
A. height and blood group: blood group is discontinuous, but height is continuous.
B. height and sex: sex is discontinuous, but height is continuous.
C. colour and weight: skin colour and weight both vary smoothly across a range, so both are continuous.

Exam tip: when a question asks for a pair, both features must qualify, so test each one separately. Ask: can I sort people into a few fixed groups, or do I need a measuring scale?

items.hint1: Two separate choices hide in these options. Is it a variation or an adaptation? And is it about body form or body function?
items.hint2: Only some people can taste this chemical, while others of the same species cannot. That makes it a difference between individuals, and nothing in the question links it to surviving in a habitat.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, decide whether tasting a chemical depends on the shape of a body part or on the way the body works.
items.solution:
Answer: B. physiological variations

Variation is the set of differences between individuals of the same species. Morphological variation is in structure and appearance, such as height, skin colour or fingerprints. Physiological variation is in how the body works, such as blood group or the ability to taste a particular chemical. An adaptation is different: it is a feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its habitat.

How to tell: phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) is a chemical that tastes bitter to some people and has little or no taste to others. The difference lies in how their taste receptors respond, not in how the tongue looks. And because it is a difference between individuals, with no survival advantage shown in a habitat, it is a variation, not an adaptation.

Why not the others:
A. morphological variations: morphological means form or structure, and tasting is not something you can see: a taster's tongue looks the same as a non-taster's.
C. morphological adaptation: PTC tasting is not a structural feature, and nothing links it to survival in a habitat.
D. physiological adaptation: it is about body function, but it is a difference between individuals with no survival advantage shown in a habitat, so it is a variation, not an adaptation.

Exam tip: split these questions into two decisions. First, variation (differences between individuals) or adaptation (a feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat)? Second, morphological (structure) or physiological (function)?

items.hint1: An allele is a form of a gene. Think about where genes are carried inside a cell.
items.hint2: A tissue is a whole group of cells, far too large a level. The nucleolus is a small body inside the nucleus whose job is making ribosomes.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, one is the control centre of the whole cell, and the other is the thread-like structure that the genes sit on. Which one is the more exact answer?
items.solution:
Answer: C. chromosomes

A gene is a short length of DNA that controls a characteristic. Alleles are different forms of the same gene, such as the allele for tallness and the allele for shortness. Genes, and so alleles, are carried on chromosomes. For most genes, a body cell carries two alleles, one at the same position, called the locus, on each chromosome of a matching pair.

How to tell: list the levels, biggest first.
Tissue → cell → nucleus → chromosome → gene
Each gene sits at its own place on a chromosome. An allele is one version of that gene, not a smaller part of it, so alleles are on the chromosomes, and the chromosomes are inside the nucleus.

Why not the others:
A. nucleus: it contains the chromosomes, but the alleles are on the chromosomes themselves, so this is not exact enough.
B. nucleolus: it is a small dense body inside the nucleus where ribosomes are made.
D. tissues: a tissue is a group of similar cells, far too large a level to be the answer.

Exam tip: when two options both seem right, choose the one that fits the exact wording of the stem. Alleles are inside the nucleus, but more exactly they are on the chromosomes.

items.hint1: Albinism is caused by a recessive allele. Start by writing down the genotype of each parent.
items.hint2: Heterozygous means each parent carries one normal allele (A) and one albino allele (a), so both parents are Aa.
items.hint3: Cross Aa with Aa in a Punnett square. Out of the four boxes, how many have two albino alleles?
items.solution:
Answer: C. ¼

Albinism is controlled by a recessive allele. A child is albino only if it receives the albino allele from both parents (aa). Heterozygous parents (Aa) have normal skin because the normal allele A is dominant, but each of them can still pass on a.

How to tell:
Let A = normal skin (dominant) and a = albino (recessive)
Parents: Aa × Aa
Gametes from each parent: A or a
Offspring: AA, Aa, Aa, aa
Only aa is albino: 1 out of 4 = ¼

Why not the others:
A. ½: this is the chance of a child being a carrier (Aa), not an albino.
B. ⅓: a single-gene cross like this gives four equally likely combinations, so the answer comes in quarters, not thirds.
D. 1: this would need both parents to be albino (aa × aa).

Exam tip: a cross between two heterozygous parents, Aa × Aa, gives an expected ratio of 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. For each child, the chance of the recessive trait showing is ¼, and of the dominant trait ¾.

items.hint1: Compare the top of the diagram with the bottom. How many DNA double helices are there at each end?
items.hint2: Protein synthesis would show a single strand of RNA and ribosomes, and a mutation would need a changed base to be pointed out, which this drawing does not do.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, think about what the process produces. The drawing starts with one double helix. What does it end with, and what would you call that?
items.solution:
Answer: C. DNA replication

DNA replication is the copying of a DNA molecule before a cell divides. The double helix unzips as the weak bonds between its base pairs break. Each old strand then acts as a template, a pattern for a new strand, and new bases pair up with it, A with T and C with G. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each made of one old strand and one new strand.

How to tell: at the top of the diagram is one double helix. In the middle it has unzipped into two separate strands with the bases sticking out. At the bottom are two complete double helices. One molecule becoming two identical molecules is replication.

Why not the others:
A. Protein synthesis: this would show a single strand of mRNA and ribosomes, not two new DNA double helices.
B. gene coding: this is not the name of a biological process. It only describes what genes do, carrying the code for proteins.
D. gene mutation: this is a change in the order of bases in DNA, while the diagram shows a normal copying process.

Exam tip: in DNA diagrams, count the molecules. One double helix becoming two double helices is replication. DNA making a single strand of mRNA is transcription, the first stage of protein synthesis.

items.hint1: In DNA the bases always pair up in a fixed way. Recall which base pairs with adenine.
items.hint2: Adenine always pairs with thymine, and cytosine always pairs with guanine.
items.hint3: Every adenine in the DNA has exactly one thymine partner on the other strand. What does that tell you about their amounts?
items.solution:
Answer: D. 32%

In double-stranded DNA, adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) always pairs with guanine (G). Because every A has exactly one T partner, the amount of A always equals the amount of T, and the amount of C always equals the amount of G.

How to tell:
A = T, so T = 32%
A + T = 32% + 32% = 64%
C + G = 100% − 64% = 36%, so C = 18% and G = 18%

Why not the others:
A. 10%: nothing in the pairing rule gives this figure. Thymine must equal adenine.
B. 16%: this is half of 32%, but thymine equals adenine, not half of it.
C. 27%: this is not equal to adenine, so it breaks the pairing rule.

Exam tip: in DNA base questions, pair first. A = T and C = G. If one base is given, its partner has the same value, and the other two bases share what is left of the 100% equally.

items.hint1: Recall Lamarck's famous example of the giraffe's long neck, and what he said caused it.
items.hint2: Lamarck published his theory in 1809, long before anyone knew about genes or mutation, so his theory could not be based on either.
items.hint3: Of the two options left, recall the second part of Lamarck's theory. Lamarck's theory had two parts. The first is about how an animal's body changes during its own life. What did he claim happens to those changes when the animal has young? Which option says that?
items.solution:
Answer: C. organisms transfer acquired characters to their offspring

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck published his theory in 1809. It had two parts. Use and disuse: parts of the body that are used a lot grow bigger and stronger, while parts that are not used grow weaker. Inheritance of acquired characters: these changes, gained during the organism's life, are passed on to its offspring. Later work showed that acquired characters are not passed on in this way, but this is still what Lamarck's theory states.

How to tell: think of Lamarck's giraffe. He said giraffes stretched their necks to reach high leaves, their necks grew longer during their lives, and their young were born with longer necks. That is an acquired character being passed on.

Why not the others:
A. characteristics of organisms are not the sum of the characters of their parents: this is not what Lamarck taught, and it says nothing about how change is passed on.
B. characteristics of organisms are determined by mutation: mutation was discovered long after Lamarck and belongs to modern genetics.
D. organism acquire genes from their parents: genes were unknown in Lamarck's time, and this describes modern genetics.

Exam tip: link each evolution scientist to one key phrase. Lamarck: use and disuse, and inheritance of acquired characters. Darwin: natural selection and survival of the fittest.

items.hint1: A honeybee colony is divided into castes, each with its own job. Think about which members lay eggs, which do the daily work, and which are male.
items.hint2: A beehive has no king. Its main egg-laying female mates with males on a flight outside the hive.
items.hint3: Between the two options left, recall the special name given to male honeybees, and check which option includes it.
items.solution:
Answer: A. drones, queen and workers

Honeybees are social insects that live in a colony divided into three castes, each with its own job. The queen is the main fertile female and lays nearly all the eggs. Workers are females that do not normally breed; they collect nectar and pollen, build the comb, feed the young and guard the hive. Drones are males whose main job is to mate with a queen.

How to tell: check the caste names against a beehive. A hive has a queen, workers and drones, with no king and no soldiers.

Why not the others:
B. workers, soldiers and reproductives: these are termite castes. Bees have no soldier caste, because the workers guard the hive.
C. soldiers, workers and king: a king and soldiers belong to a termite colony, not a beehive.
D. king, queen and soldiers: a beehive has no king and no soldiers, and this leaves out the workers.

Exam tip: keep the two social insects apart. Termites: king, queen, workers and soldiers. Honeybees: queen, workers and drones. A king or a soldier in an option means termites.

items.hint1: Match each name to what that scientist is best known for in biology.
items.hint2: Schleiden helped to found the cell theory, and Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation and made vaccines.
items.hint3: Of the two names left, one proposed use and disuse. The other proposed that nature picks out the individuals best suited to their surroundings. Which is which?
items.solution:
Answer: C. Charles Darwin

Charles Darwin formulated the theory of evolution by natural selection, and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea on his own. Darwin set it out in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859. The theory says that individuals of a species vary, more young are produced than can survive, and those with inherited features that suit their surroundings are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass those features on to their young.

How to tell: natural selection is Darwin's key phrase, just as use and disuse is Lamarck's.

Why not the others:
A. Mathias Schleiden: he was a botanist who, with Theodor Schwann, put forward the cell theory.
B. Louis Pasteur: he disproved spontaneous generation and developed vaccines and pasteurisation.
D. Jean Lamarck: he proposed use and disuse and the inheritance of acquired characters, not natural selection.

Exam tip: learn scientists as name and idea pairs. Darwin, natural selection. Lamarck, use and disuse. Schleiden and Schwann, cell theory. Pasteur, germ theory and pasteurisation. Mendel, the laws of inheritance.
